tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Natalie, a faculty member in data science and a sports scientist at UVA, argues that athlete-health research needs shared, open collectives. She and a colleague reviewed GPS wearable studies in team field sports and found no conclusive evidence for injury prediction, citing inconsistent injury tracking, poor statistical framing, and overclaiming from small samples. She still uses wearables daily and describes a men's basketball monitoring day: wellness survey, countermovement jumps on force plates, barbell tracking, and GPS in practice. She proposes a collective with ACC peers sharing best practices, code, and longitudinal data. The collective is currently an idea with funding requested.

1	=== 2022-03-25_Rn7sZ5kNsNw_using-technology-to-monitor-workload-in-elite-figure-skating/summary.md
2	---
3	type: video-summary
4	video_id: Rn7sZ5kNsNw
5	title: "SSAC22: Using Technology to Monitor Workload in Elite Figure Skating"
6	event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
7	speakers: [Lindsey Slater (caption spelling: "lindsey slater")]
8	topics: [sports-science, injury-health, other-sport:figure-skating]
9	confidence: supported
10	caption_source: auto
11	status: draft
12	---
13	
14	## Summary
15	
16	The speaker, a physical therapy professor and the sport science manager for U.S. Figure Skating, describes replacing pen-and-paper jump logs with a single hip-worn motion sensor. The first goal was to count training workload, with performance and technique feedback second, because elite athletes reject being told what to do. Three case studies show the sensor used to guide a return after puberty, to set a daily jump limit, and to test whether a skater could realistically land a triple axel by a deadline. The talk matters for athlete monitoring because it ties a device output to individual rep limits, and it shows that adoption depended on who drove the project.
17	
18	## Key claims
19	
20	- Vertical loading on a pop jump was found to match that of triple and quad jumps, so early monitoring counted every jump equally [01:32].
21	- Self-logged jump counts were unreliable: athletes skipped pop jumps and counted combinations as one [02:34].
22	- Priority one was tracking workload, not judging performance; telling an Olympic athlete what to do risks losing them [03:06].
23	- A four-sensor setup was first tested on one top athlete, and the speaker says no earlier system had captured the rotation of a triple lutz without saturating [04:38].
24	- Sensors on the full ice surface avoided the marker-system limit of jumping inside one circle [05:08].
25	- A single sensor on the hip, smaller than a smartwatch, gives immediate app feedback on jump type, revolutions, rotation speed, air time, height and timing of peak angular velocity; some outputs are estimates and loop jumps are hardest [06:40], [07:10], [07:41].
26	- Case 1 (post-puberty return): triple axel work was paused, rotation rose over months, peaked around May, dipped in July after a vaccination, and recovered by August [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
27	- Time to peak rotation moved earlier toward a point just over halfway through the jump as she improved [11:16].
28	- The second jump in a combination shows angular velocity like a triple axel, so it carries heavy rotational landing load; coaches were told to track triple-triples with triple axels and quads [12:18], [12:48].
29	- After tracking those together, the athlete had no further hip pain flare-ups [13:50].
30	- Case 2: the athlete underestimated her daily jumps; rotation fell across a two-hour session, and the concern was residual fatigue the next day [14:20], [14:51].
31	- A 75-jump daily ceiling was set, with two recovery days required if she chose to exceed it; the ceiling was raised after progressive exposure with no fatigue [15:23], [15:54], [16:24].
32	- Case 3: after about four months of data the team judged a triple axel by the target date unrealistic because her rotation appeared capped at the triple; she returned the sensor [17:25], [18:25].
33	- Adoption pattern: coach-driven succeeded, athlete-driven succeeded, practitioner-driven did not [18:55], [19:26].
34	- The work was funded by the USOPC and developed with the sensor company in about a year [19:57], [20:58].
35	
36	## Numbers and definitions
37	
38	- Triple axel rotation needed for a woman: about 1900 to 1950 degrees per second; the speaker estimates the Russians at 2000 to 2100 (estimate) [09:14].
39	- Case 1 athlete rotated about 1750 degrees per second on return in February; reached the 1900s in March [09:14], [10:16].
40	- Setup time: about 5 minutes for sensors versus an hour or more for markers; 11 sensors about 10 minutes versus 30 to 45 minutes for a marker system [05:08], [06:09].
41	- Case 2: thought she did 60 to 70 jumps a day; actual close to 100 [14:20]. Limit 75; beyond it, two days around 40 jumps [15:23], [15:54]. Later limit 85 (caption is garbled around "high low days are 85") [16:24].
42	- Five of the six single skaters at the games wore the sensor [08:13].
43	- Residual fatigue: still fatigued the next day [14:51].
44	
45	## Methods and frameworks named
46	
47	- Wearable IMU (single hip sensor, plus a four-sensor and an 11-sensor test) with app-based jump detection and an algorithm refined with more data [07:41].
48	- Peak angular velocity and time to peak, combined, as the two key measures [18:25].
49	- Individual thresholds and a progressive increase in allowed volume, compared by the speaker to progressive overload [15:54].
50	- Comparison of one athlete's trend against athletes who can land triple axels [17:55].
51	
52	## Limits and open questions
53	
54	- Three case studies, no group statistics, no accuracy figures against video.
55	- The speaker says the old jump-height finding (doubles versus triples) probably needs retesting with today's quads [02:03].
56	- Internal tension: the talk begins with "all jumps are equal" and later says not all jumps are equal [01:32], [13:19].
57	- The "no flare-ups" result is one athlete without a control [13:50].
58	- The ceiling-effect judgement in Case 3 is the speaker's belief; the athlete rejected it [17:25].
59	- The speaker is the sport science manager for the governing body, with an institutional interest.
60	- Caption problems: sensor company transcribed as "40 motion sports" and "4d sports"/"4d motion" [04:08], [06:40], [20:58]; "cheetah jump" [07:10] is probably garbled; "pear skaters" is pairs [26:18].
61	
62	## Q&A
63	
64	- Spins: not measured; loading is jump based; a boot sensor is planned for the next phase [22:06].
65	- Arms overhead: has data but keeps it private; the speaker says it reduces inertia and helps young skaters but is harder after puberty [23:10], [23:40], [24:10].
66	- Baseball pitch counts and volleyball jump counts are being explored with a single sensor [24:45], [25:16].
67	- Pairs skating: hip sensor is not workable, other locations are being discussed [26:18].
68	=== 2022-03-25_VZEYQU2-Oc8_how-data-journey-started-for-the-indianapolis-colts/summary.md

73	event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

75	topics: [front-office, decision-making, american-football]

80	
81	## Summary
82	
83	The Colts' vice president of data strategy and analytics describes how the club started a data program on the business side (ticketing, sponsorship, marketing), not on-field analytics. The team scored itself on a five-level maturity scale across five areas, interviewed staff, set two-year targets, and built a roadmap of initiatives, with a custom cloud data warehouse first. The speaker argues that technology alone does not fix data problems, and that people, process and clear goals matter as much. The Q&A covers team structure, a cross-department forum, and gaining leadership buy-in. The talk is useful as a method for assessing and sequencing data work, with no athlete data shown.
84	
85	## Key claims
86	
87	- The club began from its mission, then asked which capabilities to build or improve, with limited money and people [02:05], [02:37], [03:09].
88	- Having technology does not help without the right people to use it [03:09].
89	- A data maturity framework covered five areas (customer strategy, infrastructure, analytics, operations, performance tracking), each scored from awareness through leading [04:11], [04:42], [05:12].
90	- Interviews showed friction came from people, process and unclear goals, not only technology [06:13].
91	- Stakeholders were asked where capability needed to be in two years, which produced the gap [06:45], [07:15].
92	- The main infrastructure need was an integrated view of fans across touch points, not "a data warehouse" as such [10:19], [10:50].
93	- Designing the warehouse is partly art, since the schema must reflect strategy and use [11:20].
94	- The warehouse was sequenced as an immediate item because it enabled others [11:50].
95	- The club moved from an out-of-box solution to a custom one, and says this may not suit other organizations [12:53], [13:23].
96	- Four selection considerations: break silos, scale without third parties, faster insight, collaboration through self-serve tools [13:53], [14:24], [15:24], [15:54].
97	- Delivery: an outside firm (caption: "data climber") built it and handed over full ownership; Snowflake is the cloud warehouse; master data management gives a single view [17:57], [18:29], [19:00].
98	- Benefits claimed: customizable, IP owned, schema built for their needs, less duplication, speed and cost control [19:30], [20:01].
99	- The journey is described as never ending [20:31].
100	
101	## Numbers and definitions
102	
103	- 24 staff interviewed across commercial departments, finance, executives and ownership [05:43].
104	- Five strategic areas, two components each, so 10 capabilities; five maturity levels (awareness to leading) [04:42], [08:17].
105	- Score of 62 out of 100 on the internal assessment [08:17].
106	- Blueprint spanning about two and a half years [07:47]; stakeholders were asked about two years out [06:45].
107	- 12 initiatives in the roadmap [11:50].
108	- "Center of excellence" meets weekly [24:41].
109	
110	## Methods and frameworks named
111	
112	- Data maturity framework with questionnaires and qualitative interviews [05:12], [06:13].
113	- Gap analysis (current versus target level) turned into programs and initiatives mapped to capabilities, tagged to strategy, process, organization, technology and KPIs [07:47], [09:49], [10:19].
114	- Roadmap with layers and timelines, warehouse first [11:50].
115	- Matrix of staff skills (strategy and analytics, CRM and platforms, activation of data) tied to vertical departments, plus a cross-department center of excellence [22:05], [23:07], [24:09].
116	
117	## Limits and open questions
118	
119	- Business-side data only; no athlete, performance or injury content.
120	- Results of the program are not reported; the work was in progress at the time [20:31].
121	- The speaker says he cannot share all the initiatives [09:19]; the scoring scale and per-area scores are not shown in the captions.
122	- 62 out of 100 is an internal measure with no external benchmark; the answer about outside-industry benchmarking gives no numbers [30:29].
123	- The talk was presented under a sponsor (Sigma, per the host introduction) and names vendors chosen by the club, which is institutional and commercial context [00:01].
124	- Caption problems: "data climber", "snowflakes", "russell scabetti" and "tan" (probably the team) may be misspelled [15:54], [18:29], [29:28].
125	
126	## Q&A
127	
128	- Team structure: three staff with distinct skill sets, each tied to a department, plus a weekly center of excellence [22:05], [24:09].
129	- Second question: the audience question is garbled; the answer covers ownership's commitment, treating the group as an internal service, and building buy-in over time [25:53], [26:24], [26:55].
130	- Benchmarking: teams share practices through a league community call (caption: "russell scabetti"); the club also looks outside sports for ideas [29:28], [29:58], [30:29].
131	=== 2022-04-01_Q3i3FOC-dPE_using-tracking-and-charting-data-to-better-evaluate-nfl-play/summary.md
132	---
133	type: video-summary
134	video_id: Q3i3FOC-dPE
135	title: "SSAC22: Using Tracking and Charting Data to Better Evaluate NFL Players: A Review"
136	event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
137	speakers: [Eric Eager (introduced as being from Pro Football Focus)]
138	topics: [american-football, competitive-advantage]
139	confidence: supported
140	caption_source: auto
141	status: draft
142	---
143	
144	## Summary
145	
146	Eager argues that football analytics has used its three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, and player tracking) mostly one at a time, and that combining them gives better player evaluation. He shows three cases from Pro Football Focus (PFF): an expected pressure rate for pass rushers, a "bite distance" measure for linebackers on play action, and a speed-adjusted receiver grade for deep routes. In each case the hand-charted grade supplies the target and tracking data supplies a measure that is steadier from year to year or tracks athletic testing. The Q&A covers second-order effects, trade-offs and model context.
147	
148	## Key claims
149	
150	- Football analytics has advanced from a few public writers to many data sources, but each source is mostly used alone, and combining them would improve player evaluation [01:33].
151	- PFF charts every NFL and college game by hand, producing player grades and event labels. The NFL's tracking data comes from chips in shoulder pads and the ball [02:08, 02:40].
152	- For pass rushers, PFF's charted pressure and win-rate data served as training targets, and tracking data supplied the predictors, in two models (pressure and win rate) [06:16].
153	- The most important predictor of a pressure was the defender's vertical distance covered in the first second. The model was an XGBoost ensemble of decision trees [06:47].
154	- Charted position labels (nose tackle, edge defender) also entered the model, so it carries some information on player type [07:18].
155	- Each play yields a pressure probability, not only a yes or no [07:48].
156	- Pressure is treated as the process that leads to sacks. PFF pressure rate and expected pressure rate together predict sack rate better than either alone, and tracking data also adds power when predicting a player's own pressure rate [08:19, 08:49].
157	- Expected pressure rate tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than charted data does, which gives a time-varying athleticism measure in place of one combine number [09:19, 09:50].
158	- Coverage grades are unstable year to year. Linebacker "bite distance under expected" (BDU), the vertical displacement on play action adjusted for situation, is more predictive year to year than the coverage grade [10:20, 11:22, 12:23].
159	- Eager's reasoning for BDU: biting on a fake leaves the middle of the field open, the most valuable area to throw [10:51, 11:22].
160	- A receiver model using mean, median and max speed over a play found speed to be the most important variable for a positive PFF grade on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55].
161	- The resulting speed-adjusted grade is steadier year to year than the deep-pass grade and correlates with the 40-yard dash, with exceptions such as Landry (slow 40, good receiver) and Kupp (faster on field than his timed run) [13:55, 14:25, 14:56].
162	- Tracking data's promise may not be reached without combining it with charting and play-by-play [15:27].
163	
164	## Numbers and definitions
165	
166	- Sacks take about two points on average from an offense [05:45].
167	- Sack rate predicting itself year to year: about 0.24 (R squared), given with "I think" and "or something" [08:19].
168	- BDU is described as three or four times more predictive year to year (R squared) than the coverage grade. The captions read "about four times three or four times", so the exact multiple is garbled [11:53, 12:23].
169	- Kupp's pro-day 40 time: 4.62 (caption "cooper cup"; the speaker was unsure of the year and said 2017) [14:56].
170	- Pressure: charted when a rusher moves the quarterback off his spot or gets a sack. Win rate: charted as whether the rusher won the rep. The two are correlated but can differ [05:15, 05:45].
171	- PFF grades are discrete steps of half a point from negative two (caption wording) [26:36].
172	- First-second speed was measured in the vertical (y) direction and as straight-line distance [06:47].
173	
174	## Methods and frameworks named
175	
176	- Charted grades as labels, tracking features as predictors (pressure, win rate, receiver grade) [06:16, 13:25].
177	- XGBoost classification for pressure [06:47].
178	- Adjusting linebacker displacement for situation (run tendencies, down and distance) and averaging over time [11:22, 11:53].
179	- Year-to-year R squared as the test of whether a new measure is better than the existing grade [08:19, 12:23].
180

502	- Garbled caption names: Diggs, Kelsey, Michael Horton, Dantzler, and the quarterback named after Joe Thomas [04:37], [16:34], [23:47].
503	
504	## Q&A
505	
506	- Wanted data: quarterback progression [45:15].
507	- Z-axis: not available [46:15].
508	- Time and score context: not included [47:18].
509	- Teammate influence: gravity credit for double teams [47:49].
510	- Yards after catch context: dots and blockers [50:20].
511	- Scheme versus quarterback: cannot be separated [51:55].
512	- Predictiveness: still to be determined [53:28].
513	- Win rate to sacks: predictive, with a finishing skill separate [55:29].
514	- Route types: should be accounted for; go routes inefficient, crossing and out routes efficient [57:32].
515	=== 2023-03-15_wVUwt2A_xi0_an-analytical-framework-for-winning-the-super-bowl-presented/summary.md
516	---
517	type: video-summary
518	video_id: wVUwt2A_xi0
519	title: "SSAC23: An Analytical Framework For Winning The Super Bowl presented by SumerSports"
520	event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
521	speakers: [Jack Jones]
522	topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
523	confidence: supported
524	caption_source: auto
525	status: draft
526	---
527	
528	## Summary
529	
530	Jack Jones, co-founder and COO of SumerSports, splits football analytics into four areas: personnel selection, performance maximization, play design, and in-game decision making. He argues each is a search space too large for a person to explore, and cites estimated counts for rosters, player improvement paths, offensive plays, and game sequences. His company started with roster building. It scores a whole roster with one number, "roster value", then uses an optimizer to find the highest-value roster that fits the salary cap and player availability. The tool accepts user overrides and club-provided positional weights. The talk is a company pitch, and no accuracy results are shown.
531	
532	## Key claims
533	
534	- Football analytics can be split into four areas: personnel selection, performance maximization, play design, and in-game decision making [01:37].
535	- Personnel selection is hard because of other teams, injuries, contracts, the cap, and varying player scale [02:38].
536	- The speaker holds that no club or third party is seriously calculating a single measure of whole-roster strength, which his company calls roster value [11:22].
537	- Many metrics exist for evaluating a wide receiver, but none for a whole roster [11:54].
538	- Roster value is built from player grades, positional importance, and snap distribution, summed across the roster [12:55].
539	- The approach has three steps: define roster value, list all feasible rosters under availability and cap limits, pick the highest-value one [12:24].
540	- A roster that cannot fit under the cap is excluded from the feasible list [13:55].
541	- Signing is treated as a yes or no decision, which makes this a discrete optimization problem [14:26].
542	- The problem is too large to list every roster, so the team shapes it into a form that solves in seconds [15:27].
543	- Decision variables include "stint paths" (how a club handles a player over time, such as drafting and later cutting) and role assignments (position and depth) [15:27].
544	- The optimizer plans several future seasons, and users can weight them depending on whether they are contending or rebuilding [16:59].
545	- Users can override the system, for example by barring a signing or a draft before a given round, to cover intangibles [17:30].
546	- The system is meant to augment human decisions, not replace them [18:32].
547	- The tool uses a club's own information and tries to optimize it rather than dictate what to optimize [21:07].
548	- Positional importance has defaults but is adjusted using a club survey, because schemes differ [22:41].
549	- Cap value beyond the projection horizon is handled as assets and liabilities, such as carryover and dead money [24:47].
550	
551	## Numbers and definitions
552	
553	- Roster value: a single measure of overall roster strength [11:22]. Defined as the sum of player performance values, each built from grade, positional importance, and snaps [12:55].
554	- Roughly 150 snaps per game and 22 players on the field [01:07]. Later given as 154 plays in a game [08:17].
555	- 53-man roster [02:38]. Hypothetical GM fills 18 spots, with 35 under contract: 11 from free agency, 7 from the draft [03:08].
556	- Hypothetical pools of 100 free agents and 150 draft prospects [03:08]. The captions give "100 and 150" and the combinatorics are garbled ("1527" and "41 septillion" at [03:40]); the speaker's stated order of magnitude is 10 to the 25th rosters [03:40]. Treat the exact figure as unverified.
557	- About 100 trillion synapses [04:10]; roughly 600 muscles, 300 joints, four movements per joint, average 90 degrees of range [04:40]; roughly 65 million physical ways to execute a task, and 100 trillion plus 65 million combined ways to improve a player [05:12]. The captions garble part of this arithmetic.
558	- 36 million offensive passing plays and 17,280 running plays under the speaker's route-tree coding [06:13]. The captions garble this sentence ("36 million 17 200" at [06:45]).
559	- Chess comparison: 40 turns per game and about 30 moves per piece per turn, against 154 football plays [08:17]. Shannon's chess figure of 10 to the 120th, and about 10 to the 80th atoms in the observable universe [08:47].
560	- Average GM tenure of 2.1 years over five years, and average head coach tenure of four years [09:50].
561	- SumerSports formed in January 2022 [10:22].
562	- Over 200,000 decision variables in the optimizer [15:58].
563	- Projection horizon number: the captions give "25th season" [16:59]; this is likely a garbled year and should not be cited.
564	- Beta with two clubs, tied to the draft [20:37].
565	
566	## Methods and frameworks named
567	
568	- Four-quadrant framework for football analytics [01:37].
569	- Roster value built from player grades, positional importance, and snap distribution [12:55].
570	- Integer programming (a kind of discrete optimization), reformulated as a convex, linear problem to solve in seconds [14:57, 15:27].
571	- Stint paths and role assignments as decision variables; multi-season projection with user weighting [15:58, 16:59].
572	- User constraints and club-supplied positional importance via a survey [17:30, 22:41].
573	- A team member with ten years of club experience supplies cap knowledge [24:14].
574	- The product name appears in the captions as "Marvel" (caption spelling).
575	
576	## Limits and open questions
577	
578	- No accuracy, back-test, or example roster results are shown. Evidence is the speaker's description.
579	- How player grades are produced and combined across positions is not described.
580	- When asked whether linearizing and convexifying the problem loses optimality, the speaker said he was not the optimization expert and offered to follow up [21:37]. The question was not answered.
581	- The search-space counts are rough, partly garbled in the captions, and describe size, not quality of decisions.
582	- The speaker's claims about competitors and market gaps are the company's own view.
583	- The tool covered the draft in beta at the time, with a year-round tool in development [23:12].
584	- Method for market value and contract cost: only cap handling is described, not how player prices are estimated [24:14].
585	- The talk concerns NFL cap and roster structure and may not transfer to college.
586	
587	## Q&A
588	
589	- Would the company work in other leagues such as the NBA? Football focus for now, others possible later [20:04].
590	- Are some teams more data driven or more resistant? A beta with two clubs; interest varies; the tool uses club information [20:37].
591	- Does linearizing or convexifying the integer program make results suboptimal? Acknowledged a trade-off, deferred to the optimization team [21:37].
592	- Is positional value set by the club's scheme? Yes, defaults plus a club survey [22:11].
593	- Is the tool year-round? Currently draft-focused, working toward a year-round tool [23:12].
594	- How are market value and cap effects handled? Cap handling by a former club staffer; beyond-horizon effects via assets and liabilities [23:43].
595	=== 2024-03-20_1nt8hK2oYrE_feeling-the-pressure-a-unified-framework-for-automating-pass/summary.md
596	---
597	type: video-summary
598	video_id: 1nt8hK2oYrE
599	title: "SSAC24:Feeling the Pressure: A Unified Framework for Automating Pass Rushing Statistics in NFL Games"
600	event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
601	speakers: [S Min Hong (caption spelling; introduced as "s Min Hong", an applied scientist at AWS)]
602	topics: [american-football, other:player-tracking]
603	confidence: supported
604	caption_source: auto
605	status: draft
606	---
607	
608	## Summary
609	
610	An applied scientist from AWS presents work done with the NFL's Next Gen Stats team on measuring pass-rush pressure throughout a play instead of only counting sacks, hits, and hurries at the end. The framework has three parts: identify who is rushing and who is blocking, match each rusher to blockers, and estimate a pressure score between 0 and 1 at each moment. It uses public tracking data from the Big Data Bowl and labels from PFF. The speaker reports high F1 scores for the first two parts, picked a random forest for the pressure score because of better calibration, and shows example plays. Evaluation of the pressure score is only by proxy.
611	
612	## Key claims
613	
614	- Existing pass-rush statistics record only end results, so players who got close but did not finish the play get no credit [01:02].
615	- The aim is to measure pressure continuously across a play and give credit to players who apply it [01:34].
616	- Three technical problems are addressed: separating rushers from blockers, matching them, and estimating pressure over time [03:10].
617	- Automating blocker and rusher labeling replaces hand labeling of video clips, saving cost and labor [06:15].
618	- Two models were promising for the identification tasks, and the speaker went with AutoGluon-style models, spelled "Orum" and "autog glom" in the captions (caption spelling) [07:17].
619	- A graph neural network performed worse but was kept as a future direction because one model can handle both tasks [08:17].
620	- The pressure score is modeled as a probability on a 0 to 1 scale at any moment in the play [09:19].
621	- A random forest was chosen over neural or transformer models for better calibration [12:28].
622	- In sample plays, the score shows different players creating pressure early and late, and credits two players where the human label credited one [13:00, 14:04].
623	- Derived outputs include pressure time and a high-pressure zone above a 75 percent threshold [14:34].
624	- Rusher distance to the passer and the number of open rushers were the main factors the speaker gave [18:08].
625	
626	## Numbers and definitions
627	
628	- F1 of 0.99 for blocker and rusher identification and about 0.91 for matchups (captions: "0.99" and "close 0.91") [07:47]. The captions are rough, so the exact values may differ.
629	- Pressure score: instantaneous probability, on a 0 to 1 scale, of a rusher producing a hit, hurry, or sack [09:19].
630	- High-pressure zone: time above a 75 percent threshold [14:34].
631	- Blocker interference feature: count of offensive blockers within an area of interest between rusher and passer, defined by distance and angle [10:23].
632	- Target variables: PFF hurry, hit, sack labels, plus an engineered distance-based label [10:54]. The speaker's example: a rusher within one yard of the passer before one second [20:39] (garbled in captions, so the exact rule is uncertain).
633	- No accuracy figures are stated for the final pressure score. Evaluation was a proxy based on maximum pressure compared with PFF labels [11:26].
634	- Calibration measured with expected and maximum calibration error [12:28]; no values given.
635	
636	## Methods and frameworks named
637	
638	- Data: Big Data Bowl tracking data (positions, velocity, acceleration, player IDs, play outcomes) from the NFL Next Gen Stats team and AWS [04:12, 04:42].
639	- Static features (initial positions, roles) and dynamic features (position, velocity, acceleration, direction), standardized before modeling [06:46].
640	- Sequential models: identify blockers and rushers, then match them [07:47].
641	- Random forest probability model for pressure, with the engineered blocker interference feature [09:51, 12:28].
642	- Ground truth for who blocks whom came from hand labels by the NFL and PFF [19:08].
643	
644	## Limits and open questions
645	
646	- Pressure score accuracy is not quantified in the captions; only a proxy evaluation is described [11:26].
647	- The speaker said model performance differed across player groups and there is room to improve [11:58]. The captions are garbled here.
648	- The model did not account for team scheme or blocking and rushing strategy [15:34].
649	- It does not attribute pressure to specific players: the speaker said they did not try to separate whose pressure it is [21:40], although the demonstration credits individual players.
650	- No correlation check against quarterback motion was done [23:13].
651	- The speaker acknowledged complex position features were not modeled [18:38].
652	- Several names and model names are garbled (Orum, autog glom, "Parson").
653	
654	## Q&A
655	
656	- Which is harder to find, a pass blocker or a pass rusher? Not answered directly; the speaker described which features drive pressure, mostly rusher distance, velocity, acceleration, and open lanes [17:37].
657	- What was the ground truth for who blocks whom? Hand labels from the NFL and PFF; handles double and triple teams [19:08].
658	- Should the metric favor how fast pressure arrives? Agreed; the target added a distance-and-time rule [20:09].
659	- How does it disentangle which player the pressure comes from? It does not; the target is forgiving to credit rushers in a threshold area [21:40].
660	- Was the score checked against quarterback motion? Not done; relative velocity features were used [23:13].

1	=== 2024-03-20_4oKByRaArVs_research-collectives-the-call-for-large-scale-open-science-i/summary.md
2	---
3	type: video-summary
4	video_id: 4oKByRaArVs
5	title: "SSAC24: Research Collectives: The Call for Large-Scale, Open Science Initiatives in Sports Science"
6	event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
7	speakers: [Natalie (surname not stated), host introduced as Grant anhorn (caption spelling)]
8	topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making]
9	confidence: supported
10	caption_source: auto
11	status: draft
12	---
13	
14	## Summary
15	
16	Natalie, a faculty member in data science and a sports scientist at UVA, argues that athlete-health research needs shared, open collectives. She and a colleague reviewed GPS wearable studies in team field sports and found no conclusive evidence for injury prediction, citing inconsistent injury tracking, poor statistical framing, and overclaiming from small samples. She still uses wearables daily and describes a men's basketball monitoring day: wellness survey, countermovement jumps on force plates, barbell tracking, and GPS in practice. She proposes a collective with ACC peers sharing best practices, code, and longitudinal data. The collective is currently an idea with funding requested.
17	
18	## Key claims
19	
20	- Wearables spread across US teams around 2015 with promises of better performance, workload tracking, and injury prediction [02:01].
21	- Machine learning became easy to use, and papers confirming injury prediction with wearables followed [02:31].
22	- A review of GPS in team field sports found no conclusive evidence for using wearables to predict injury [03:03].
23	- Reasons: different injury-tracking methods across papers, treating injury as a pure prediction problem, and ambitious claims from small samples [03:33, 04:03].
24	- Overclaiming comes from both technology companies and researchers, partly because of publishing incentives [04:33].
25	- Coaches' stories that technology helps are useful for generating hypotheses [05:05].
26	- The program aims to optimize readiness and performance, expecting fewer fatigue and overuse injuries as a side effect [06:06].
27	- Countermovement jumps on force plates assess neuromuscular readiness, and strategy changes reveal fatigue that jump height hides [08:39].
28	- Daily data feeds coach-facing dashboards that inform lifting adjustments [09:09].
29	- The speaker holds that there is more signal in readiness than in injury [12:09].
30	- Sports research mostly sits low on the evidence hierarchy because randomized trials are hard, samples are small, and methods and data are rarely shared [13:11, 13:41].
31	- A collective could bring best practices, FAIR principles, multi-site research, and longitudinal tracking, including across the transfer portal and after careers [16:16, 17:48].
32	- Needs: funding, data architecture and agreements, oversight and consent, governance, metadata [18:19, 18:49].
33	- Athletic departments usually worry about giving away competitive advantage; the speaker argues the advantage is gone by the time academics publish, especially for health and safety data [19:56].
34	- The wellness data at her program has never made it into models, but works as a conversation starter [21:59].
35	- The speaker says she cares more about products people use daily than about papers [26:07].
36	
37	## Numbers and definitions
38	
39	- Wearables emerged in US teams around 2015 [02:01].
40	- Reviewed studies had single teams of about 15 people for one season [04:03].
41	- A player gained 24 pounds of muscle while lowering body fat and raising vertical jump [06:37]. Captions say "24 pounds of basically pure muscle"; this is the speaker's description.
42	- FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable [16:47].
43	- Evidence hierarchy: expert opinion at the bottom, then observational research, then cohort studies, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses; randomized trials are hard in sport [12:41, 13:11].
44	- She says "maybe 2%" of the room reads academic papers [15:45]; this is an offhand estimate.
45	- Collective idea discussed for about four years [24:02].
46	
47	## Methods and frameworks named
48	
49	- Review of GPS wearables in team field sports with a co-author (caption spelling "Jay hurdle") [03:03].
50	- UVA daily session: wellness questionnaire, optional smart ring, dashboards, countermovement jump on force plates, Perch barbell velocity camera, Catapult GPS worn between the shoulder blades, evening database for coaches [07:38 to 11:09].
51	- Overuse injury model credited to "koven" (caption spelling), described as open source [11:39]; a UVA model focused on optimal readiness [12:09].
52	- Hierarchy of evidence pyramid [12:41].
53	- FAIR principles, shared code instead of shared data, federated learning, a partner with data governance [16:47, 17:17, 25:05].
54	- UVA Sports Science and Analytics Collective, with an ACC peer effort [14:11, 14:43].
55	
56	## Limits and open questions
57	
58	- The review's details are not shown: how many studies, which databases, or which effect sizes. Only the conclusion is given.
59	- The basketball example was chosen to avoid privacy issues [05:35]; no injury results are shown.
60	- The claim that readiness work reduces overuse injuries is the speaker's expectation, not a tested result [06:06].
61	- Collective status: an idea with funding applied for, and peer schools may meet to judge feasibility [23:31, 24:02].
62	- Privacy and governance are unresolved [24:32].
63	- The speaker acknowledged she should run A/B tests on dashboards [26:07].
64	- Several names are caption spellings.
65	
66	## Q&A
67	
68	- Do coaches and athletic departments fear giving away secrets, and could pro players associations mandate this? Fear is the usual obstacle; advantage fades; pros already do league-level research [19:26].
69	- How does the human element fit with digital athlete data? Wellness data is a conversation starter; the speaker wants humans kept in the loop [20:58, 21:59].
70	- What stage is the collective at? An idea, funding requested, peer meeting planned [23:31].
71	- What about privacy? Plan to use a partner with governance, possibly federated learning [24:32].
72	- How does research return to coaches and athletes? Build daily-use products, get immediate feedback, include athletes as users [25:35].
73	=== 2024-03-20_6zBmxq4L6nc_evolution-of-basketball-analytics-20-years-of-nerds-data-eff/summary.md
74	---
75	type: video-summary
76	video_id: 6zBmxq4L6nc
77	title: "SSAC24: Evolution of Basketball Analytics: 20 Years of Nerds, Data, & Efficiency"
78	event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
79	speakers: [Dean Oliver, Britany donalson (caption spelling), Mike Zaron (caption spelling), Allison fiser (caption spelling), Ben Alamar (moderator)]
80	topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
81	confidence: supported
82	caption_source: auto
83	status: draft
84	---
85	
86	## Summary
87	
88	A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.
89	
90	## Key claims
91	
92	- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
93	- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
94	- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
95	- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
96	- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]
97	- A Celtics anecdote: the team was first in defensive field goal percentage by design while packing the paint, yet tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed, and a coach answered that the point is to score baskets. [13:25]
98	- Tracking data changed what analysts could tell coaches, since a box score cannot say what happened and the coaches' instructions in practice are mostly not in it. [16:55] [17:56]
99	- The first tracking data in a real NBA game was messy (players teleporting, misidentified), yet showed how far players ran and let the team change training right away. [18:58] [19:28]
100	- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
101	- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
102	- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]
103	- In player development, one panelist says direct use of data with players is limited: the technology is not there yet and presenting data is not always the best coaching tool. [29:43] [30:13]
104	- The same panelist says data is better used to design the player's environment (for example plays and reads that send a player left), which is described as a bit of behavioral science. [31:15] [31:46]
105	- Practice data is thin, practices are few and drills are not structured enough for a computer to track. [32:16] [32:46] [37:25]
106	- Tracking now lets staff check many instances of a skill such as screen setting across a game instead of cutting tape for two or three. Players who sit on the bench get no game data. [36:24] [36:54]
107	- Roster building has a largely unexploited area: culture and what kind of teammate a player might be. [34:19] [34:50]
108	- Things that did not work: teams that shoot threes indiscriminately without counting what it is like to be a player who never touches the ball; and VR headsets that made users dizzy and nauseous. [26:36] [28:09]
109	- Predictions: pose data will bring biomechanical applications, automated officiating will arrive quickly (fouls are harder), and coaching analytics could measure how staff spend practice and film time. [41:32] [42:35] [43:05] [44:38]
110	- Interviews and conversations with a player's teammates and coaches are data, and a team needs a process to judge the reliability and usefulness of that data, as with three point percentage. [46:40] [48:44]
111	- A panelist says teams sometimes lean on basketball data over qualitative data when they should not. [47:10]
112	- Dean Oliver says he would have been most surprised by how fast the game changed and how differently it is played. [49:15]
113	
114	## Numbers and definitions
115	
116	- Basketball on Paper published in 2004 and the four factors introduced in it; the four factors are not named in the talk. [02:01] [04:38]
117	- NCAA season box scores back to 1983, received on paper, about 1,200 pages (caption "1,200 pages"); a later aside says "1400 pages". [05:39] [06:42]
118	- NBA efficiency as described: adding box score stats together. [10:16]
119	- Celtics: first in defensive field goal percentage, tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed (caption). [13:25]
120	- Tracking timeline: cameras in a few arenas including Dallas, Boston and OKC, then all 30 arenas, stated for 2010 to 2016. [14:25]
121	- First NBA tracking data from playoff games in 2010. [18:58]
122	- Hawkeye: 20 to 30 data points on a body instead of a single point. [28:40]
123	- Pose data: "22 body parts at 60 Herz" (caption); the next sentences on frame rate are garbled and not reliable. About five months of that data exists, of varying quality. [41:01] [41:32] [42:03]
124	- Coaching time split described as "8020" (caption); what the two categories are is not clear. [44:38]
125	- "About 50 things" can be checked about screen setting. [36:24]
126	- Schedule color: "three" practices in January; "five games and seven nights in five cities". [32:46] [33:16]
127	- One possession out of the "50" a player was in, used to show a mislabeled matchup barely changed a game score. [22:33]
128	- Panel banter in the introduction: a career win shares per 48 of 0.138 for one panelist and a three-point attempt rate given as "64" (caption drops the decimal). Not offered as findings. [03:06] [03:37]
129	
130	## Methods and frameworks named
131	
132	- Possession-based estimation and the four factors.
133	- Box score composites (NBA efficiency) as the approach being criticized.
134	- Draft models built from typed-in NCAA box scores. [06:10]
135	- Optical tracking from camera systems (Stats LLC cameras, Second Spectrum with its own cameras, later Hawkeye), with machine learning to label plays and human quality checks. [14:25] [21:02] [21:33]
136	- Play filters linked to video for verification. [22:03]
137	- Pose or skeletal tracking and possible eye-tracking goggles as future tools. [41:01] [44:06]
138	- Environment design as a way to use data with players. [31:15]
139	- Coaching analytics: measuring what staff spend practice and film time on. [44:38]
140	
141	## Limits and open questions
142	
143	- No datasets, sample sizes, accuracy figures or results were shown; nearly all claims are experiences and opinions.
144	- Speakers are team executives, a coach and an author, each with an institutional or commercial interest (one panelist promotes a book). [35:53]

332	## Summary
333	
334	The presenters propose a team-selection model for soccer that tries to cut injuries without giving up points. Each player gets a skill rating and a next-match injury probability. A Monte Carlo tree search then simulates the coming weeks to choose the starting eleven, treating the coach's job as a sequential decision problem. Tested on open Premier League data against a greedy pick-the-best-team-each-week baseline, the model reduced simulated injuries while keeping expected points similar, and the speakers argue real managers lean toward short-term choices. They state the work is a decision framework built on public data, not a clinical prediction tool.
335	
336	## Key claims
337	
338	- The work was motivated by crowded schedules; after the winter World Cup, injury severity rose and injury costs reached very large figures [01:01].
339	- Each player has a skill rating and an injury probability, and a search over team selections balances winning now against injury risk later [02:01].
340	- Resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, but the coach has to pick the right moment [03:02].
341	- Short-term and long-term workload and detailed injury history contributed most to the injury model, ahead of travel, rain, days since last injury, temperature and age [04:33].
342	- The team-level scoring model was modified to use player skill values and matched the original model within margins of error over two seasons [06:06].
343	- Compared with a greedy selection, the search model kept similar expected points while lowering injuries for the squad and the ideal starting eleven [11:14].
344	- Real managers' selections were more similar to the greedy model than to the search model; the speakers suggest short-term pressure as the reason [10:43].
345	- In higher injury-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy one on season points, while the margin of injury reduction shrank [12:15].
346	- Real technical directors often decide for short-term gains rather than long-term athlete protection [14:48].
347	- The presenters conclude teams can rest athletes and reduce injury risk without sacrificing results [14:48].
348	
349	## Numbers and definitions
350	
351	- 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup [01:01].
352	- Almost $770 million in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season [01:01]. The conclusion later says "nearly $800 million" [12:46]; the two spoken figures differ and the captions do not reconcile them.
353	- 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season [01:01].
354	- Injury model: gradient-boosted trees (caption spelling "XG boost") on 2017-18 Premier League data plus a career injury dataset [03:02]; injury durations sampled from a Gaussian distribution fitted to real injury data [03:32].
355	- Expected points come from an adapted Maher model, which assumes scoring rates follow a Poisson distribution [05:05]; team identity features were replaced with player skill values from a contribution model captioned "VAPE" [05:36].
356	- Data: StatsBomb event data for the 17/18 and 18/19 Premier League seasons, Transfermarkt for injury history, Capology for salary [09:11].
357	- Injury model test: 70/30 split with cross-validation (captioned "five-block"), log loss 0.16 [09:11]; Pearson correlation 0.77 with observed 18/19 outcomes [09:42].
358	- Selection similarity to real coaches: about 76% for the search model, 82% for the greedy model [10:12].
359	- Brighton: 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least benefited at 7.5% for the ideal eleven [11:14].
360	- Average across Premier League teams: 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal eleven [11:44].
361	- Risk multipliers of two and three times; 1.8% more expected points at three times [12:15].
362	- Salary cost tied to predicted injuries: 22% reduction for Brighton, about 11% on average [13:16].
363	- Headline: approximately 13% fewer injuries and an 11% reduction in injury-related costs [14:18]. Inference: the 13% matches the ideal-eleven average, not the 4.6% squad figure; the speaker did not say which. The captions may also garble "five-block."

367	- Markov decision process framing of the coach's selection problem, solved approximately with Monte Carlo tree search using an upper-confidence heuristic and progressive broadening [06:37] [07:38] [08:09].
368	- Simulation assumes the coach picks the most qualified team in the rolled-out season; values are propagated back to the root [08:09].
